kept.claim: Ruby has no method overloading: the second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` silently replaces the 5-arg `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})`, so `Jobs::ResizeEmoji` calling `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` now raises ArgumentError (5 for 3..4).
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] Second `downsize` definition overwrites the first and breaks `Jobs::ResizeEmoji`

**Severity:** HIGH — custom emoji resizing raises `ArgumentError` on every run.

### The Problem

```ruby
# app/models/optimized_image.rb:145
def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})
  optimize("downsize", from, to, "#{max_width}x#{max_height}", opts)
end

# app/models/optimized_image.rb:149
def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})
  optimize("downsize", from, to, dimensions, opts)
end
```

The PR defines `OptimizedImage.downsize` twice with different arities, as if Ruby dispatched by argument count.

### Theory / Proof

Ruby has no method overloading. A later `def` with the same name on the same receiver replaces the earlier one (with `-w`, Ruby prints `warning: method redefined; discarding old downsize`). Once the class body has loaded, only the 3..4-arity version exists.

Existing caller, `app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14`:

```ruby
OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)
```

That is 5 positional arguments against a method that accepts at most 4, so it raises `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 5, expected 3..4)`. Emoji are no longer resized, and the job errors and retries in Sidekiq.

### What happens today vs. what will break

The new controller call `downsize(path, path, "80%", opts)` works only because it happens to match the surviving definition. Every 5-arg caller is broken, and nothing in the diff updates them.

### Research

Ruby language docs ("Methods", overriding): redefining a method replaces it. Idiomatic Ruby uses distinct names or optional/keyword arguments for this.

### Recommendation

Keep one method and give the new behaviour its own name, or accept a dimensions string in the existing one:

```ruby
def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})
  optimize("downsize", from, to, "#{max_width}x#{max_height}", opts)
end

def self.downsize_by(from, to, dimensions, opts={})   # e.g. "80%"
  optimize("downsize", from, to, dimensions, opts)
end
```

Then update `uploads_controller.rb:67` to call `downsize_by`. Also add a spec for `Jobs::ResizeEmoji` or `OptimizedImage.downsize` with width/height.
kept.evidence: optimized_image.rb:145-151: the two `def self.downsize` definitions are on the same class, so the second replaces the first. resize_emoji.rb:14 calls downsize with 5 positional args (opts is a plain Hash), which raises ArgumentError (5 for 3..4). The diff does not update this caller.

kept.claim: Hard-coding `maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024` for every upload type drops the client-side `max_attachment_size_kb`/`max_image_size_kb` checks, so oversized attachments are sent and only rejected by the server, and sites that allow more than 10 MB can no longer upload those files.
kept.body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] Client-side size limit hard-coded to 10 MB for all upload types, ignoring site settings

**Severity:** MEDIUM — attachment limits are no longer checked client-side, and admins' limits above 10 MB are silently capped.

### The Problem

```js
// utilities.js:181-182
var fileSizeKB = file.size / 1024;
var maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024; // 10MB
```

Before, this read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so it honoured both `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` (both `client: true`, default 3072, `config/site_settings.yml:513-518`). The same constant is hard-coded again in the 413 handler at `utilities.js:246`, and on the server `FileHelper.download(url, 10.megabytes, ...)` is used at `uploads_controller.rb:55`.

### Theory / Proof

The feature only needs to relax the *image* limit, because only images get the new server-side downsizing loop, which is guarded by `FileHelper.is_image?(filename)` at `uploads_controller.rb:64`. Attachments are not downsized, yet their client check is also replaced:

- **Attachments (default 3 MB):** a 9 MB PDF now passes the client check, is fully uploaded, and only then fails in `Validators::UploadValidator#maximum_attachment_file_size`. That wastes bandwidth, and the user sees a later, different error.
- **Sites with limits above 10 MB:** an admin who set `max_attachment_size_kb = 51200` (and raised nginx `client_max_body_size`) now has every file over 10 MB rejected in the browser with "max 10240 kB". The setting no longer does anything above 10 MB, and the 413 message reports 10240 kB whatever the proxy is actually configured to.

### What happens today vs. what will break

With defaults (3 MB and the sample nginx 10m), images of 3-10 MB now get through, which is what the PR wants. Attachments and any non-default configuration regress.

### Recommendation

Relax only the image check, and keep configured limits that are already higher:

```js
var maxSizeKB = Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'];
if (type === 'image' || Discourse.Utilities.isAnImage(file.name)) {
  maxSizeKB = Math.max(maxSizeKB, 10 * 1024); // server downsizes large images
}
```

Better still, add a site setting (for example `max_image_upload_size_before_downsize_kb`) and use it in the JS, in the 413 handler and in the `FileHelper.download` call instead of three separate literals.
kept.evidence: utilities.js:182 swaps the per-type site setting for 10*1024. validateUploadedFile is used for both images and attachments (composer.js.es6:340, mixins/upload.js.es6:41). Server-side downsizing is images-only (uploads_controller.rb:64). The 413 handler (:246) and FileHelper.download (uploads_controller.rb:55) are hard-coded too. The existing test test/javascripts/lib/utilities-test.js.es6:52-61 (max_image_size_kb=5) now fails.

kept.claim: For GIFs with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, `downsize` goes to `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`, which gifsicle rejects because it needs WxH, so large animated GIFs are never reduced; with the setting off, `convert #{from}[0]` keeps only the first frame and silently removes the animation.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] Automatic downsizing is broken for GIFs: gifsicle rejects `80%`, and the non-animated path drops all frames but the first

**Severity:** MEDIUM — large animated GIFs are either never shrunk (and then rejected) or silently turned into static images.

### The Problem

```ruby
OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)
```

`OptimizedImage.optimize` picks the instruction set by extension:

```ruby
method_name += "_animated" if !!opts[:allow_animation] && from =~ /\.GIF$/i
```

**Case A, `allow_animated_thumbnails = true`:** `downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which produces

```
gifsicle <from> --colors=256 --resize-fit 80% --optimize=3 --output <to>
```

gifsicle's `--resize-fit WxH` expects a geometry of the form `WxH` (with `_` for an unconstrained side), not a percentage. gifsicle exits non-zero, `convert_with` returns `false`, and the file is unchanged. The loop runs gifsicle 5 times for nothing, and the upload is then rejected by `UploadValidator` as too large.

Rack multipart tempfiles and `FileHelper.download` both keep the original extension, and `allow_animated_thumbnails` defaults to `true`, so this is the default path for GIF uploads. For scaling by a factor, gifsicle provides `--scale`.

**Case B, setting false:** `downsize_instructions` runs `convert #{from}[0] ... -resize 80%\>`. The `[0]` frame selector keeps only the first frame, so an animated GIF over the limit is stored as a still image without any warning.

### What happens today vs. what will break

JPEG and PNG work. Animated GIFs, which are the images most likely to be large, either fail or lose their animation.

### Recommendation

Pass a geometry every backend understands, computed from the real dimensions, and skip GIFs if animation cannot be kept:

```ruby
if tempfile && tempfile.size > 0 && SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb > 0 && FileHelper.is_image?(filename) && filename !~ /\.gif$/i
  attempt = 5
  while attempt > 0 && File.size(tempfile.path) > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes
    w, h = FastImage.size(tempfile.path)
    break unless w && h
    break unless OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, (w * 0.8).floor, (h * 0.8).floor, allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)
    attempt -= 1
  end
end
```
kept.evidence: uploads_controller.rb:67 passes "80%" to downsize. allow_animated_thumbnails defaults to true (site_settings.yml:574). The .gif extension is kept on Rack and FileHelper tempfiles, so optimize (:153-157) chooses the gifsicle `--resize-fit 80%` path. gifsicle takes WxH there (use --scale for factors), so it exits non-zero and convert_with returns false. With the setting off, `convert from[0]` (:126-135) keeps only the first frame.

kept.claim: The loop checks `tempfile.size` (fstat on the Tempfile's open descriptor), but `convert_with` runs `ImageOptim#optimize_image!`, which replaces the file at `tempfile.path` by atomic rename; the Tempfile descriptor then points at the old inode, so the size check and the `filesize` passed to `Upload.create_for` are stale.
kept.body:
## [ISSUE] `tempfile.size` is read from a stale file descriptor after the in-place downsize

**Severity:** MEDIUM — the loop's size check and the stored `upload.filesize` can be wrong, causing extra downsizing passes or wrong metadata.

### The Problem

```ruby
while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes
  OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)
  attempt -= 1
end
...
upload = Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, tempfile.size, ...)
```

### Theory / Proof

- `Tempfile#size` on an open Tempfile calls `File#size` on its open descriptor, which is `fstat(fd)`. It does not `stat` the path.
- `OptimizedImage.convert_with` first runs `convert ... to`. ImageMagick opens the output with `fopen("wb")`, which truncates the same inode, so up to this point the descriptor still reflects the new data.
- It then runs `ImageOptim.new.optimize_image!(to)`. In image_optim (0.20.2 in `Gemfile.lock`), `optimize_image!` calls `ImagePath::Optimized#replace`, which writes to a temp file in the same directory and `rename`s it over the destination. After that, `tempfile.path` names a **new inode**, while the Tempfile's descriptor still refers to the old, unlinked one that holds the pre-optimisation `convert` output.

So after the first iteration, `tempfile.size` returns the size before image_optim ran, not the size of the file on disk:

1. The loop can keep downsizing an image that is already under the limit, costing resolution and CPU time.
2. `Upload.create_for` gets that stale `tempfile.size` as `filesize`. Its `UploadValidator#maximum_file_size` compares that value, so a file that is really small enough can be rejected. `FastImage.new(file)` (upload.rb:71) also reads through the Tempfile IO, so it reads the old inode. (`Digest::SHA1.file` and storage open by path, so they see the new file.) This happens whenever image_optim actually shrinks the file, which is the normal case when the optimizer binaries are installed.

### Recommendation

Measure the file by path, and pass that size on:

```ruby
while attempt > 0 && File.size(tempfile.path) > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes
  break unless OptimizedImage.downsize(...)
  attempt -= 1
end

tempfile = File.open(tempfile.path) # or reopen the Tempfile
upload = Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, filename, File.size(tempfile.path), ...)
```
kept.evidence: Tempfile#size is fstat on the open fd. convert_with runs convert and then ImageOptim#optimize_image! (image_optim 0.20.2), which atomically renames a new file over the path, so the fd points at the old inode. The loop condition (:66) and the filesize passed at :72 (checked by UploadValidator:84) can be stale. FastImage.new(file) (upload.rb:71) reads the old inode. Digest::SHA1.file and storage open by path, so they see the new file.

kept.claim: The return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is ignored, so when convert/gifsicle fails (corrupt image, unsupported format, missing binary) the loop keeps re-running the same failing subprocess on an unchanged file, up to 5 attempts in total, instead of stopping.
kept.body:
## [OPTIMIZATION] Downsize loop ignores failure and keeps spawning subprocesses

**Severity:** LOW — wasted CPU and latency on failing uploads, which an attacker can trigger with up to 10 MB inputs.

### The Problem

```ruby
attempt = 5
while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes
  OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)
  attempt -= 1
end
```

`OptimizedImage.convert_with` returns `false` when the command exits non-zero, and also on any exception. When that happens the file is unchanged, so every later pass does exactly the same work and fails the same way.

### Theory / Proof

Each pass runs `convert` (up to 10 MB input, full decode and encode) plus `ImageOptim` (several external optimisers). That happens inside the request, or inside `Scheduler::Defer`, a single background thread shared by the process, so 5 failing passes on one upload hold up other deferred work. The upload is also re-encoded up to 5 times, and each lossy JPEG pass loses more quality.

### Recommendation

```ruby
while attempt > 0 && File.size(tempfile.path) > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes
  break unless OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)
  attempt -= 1
end
```

Also consider computing a single scale factor from `sqrt(max_bytes / current_bytes)` so one pass is usually enough.
kept.evidence: uploads_controller.rb:65-69 ignores downsize's return value. convert_with (optimized_image.rb:160-168) returns false on failure and leaves the file unchanged, so the loop runs the same failing command up to 5 times in total, on a request thread or in Scheduler::Defer.
